source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models
finding: LATS runs MCTS over agent actions. Each node is a state. It expands n children, scores them with an LM value plus self-consistency, takes real environment feedback, and writes a verbal reflection after a failed rollout. It beat ReAct, Reflexion, ToT and RAP on most tasks with GPT-3.5.
numbers: HotPotQA EM (100 questions, GPT-3.5, n=5, k=50): ReAct 0.32, Reflexion 0.51, ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54, LATS(ReAct) 0.63, LATS(n=10) 0.65, LATS(CoT+ReAct) 0.71. HumanEval GPT-3.5 pass@1: ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. MBPP GPT-3.5: Reflexion 70.0, LATS 81.1. WebShop (50 tasks): ReAct score 53.8 / SR 28.0; Reflexion 64.2 / 35.0; LATS 75.9 / 38.0.
limits: Small test sets (HotPotQA 100 questions, WebShop 50 tasks). Gain on HumanEval GPT-4 over Reflexion is only 1.7 points (about 3 of 164 problems). Self-reported, by the method authors. Higher compute than simple prompting.
agent_relevance: This is the founding claim for S6 with real feedback: search plus value plus reflection beats a single try. The sizes are modest on strong models, so treat the large GPT-3.5 gains as an upper bound.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS ablations (Table 8, Table 9, appendix)
finding: Removing parts of LATS shows which parts carry the gain. The LM value function matters most. Plain DFS with pruning loses most of the gain. Reflection adds a smaller amount.
numbers: HotPotQA EM, n=5, k=50: full LATS 0.63; no LM heuristic 0.37 (-0.26); DFS variant 0.42 (-0.21); no reflection 0.58 (-0.05). Reflexion gains 0.19 over ReAct on its own, so reflection and search overlap. Exploration weight w=0.5 gave 0.55; w=2.0 gave 0.63 (faster convergence). Depth d=4 gave 0.62.
limits: Ablations on one task (HotPotQA, 100 questions) with one model (GPT-3.5). Appendix Table 11 text extraction was garbled; main Table 8 values are used here.
agent_relevance: Most of S6's value comes from a usable value signal, then from keeping a tree rather than one line. Reflection is the cheapest add-on but gives the least. Do not drop the value step.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS cost and limits (Table 9, Table 10, appendix B)
finding: LATS claims equal sample complexity O(kn) to ToT and RAP but fewer nodes expanded on success. It admits higher cost than simple prompting and a need to revert to earlier states in the environment.
numbers: HotPotQA at k=10: ToT 0.34 with 33.97 nodes; RAP 0.44 with 31.53 nodes; LATS 0.44 with 28.42 nodes. Tokens on success about 176,500 (LATS) vs 210,215 (RAP). Equal-sample comparison: ReAct best of k=250 got 0.42; CoT-SC 0.40; LATS (n=1,k=50) 0.48; LATS (n=5,k=50) 0.63.
limits: Node counts are for successful runs only, so failed-run cost is hidden. The authors state the method assumes the environment can be reset to a prior state.
agent_relevance: Fair compute matching is the key test for any claim about search. Even here best-of-250 reaches 0.42 against 0.63, so search helped beyond sampling in this one setting. Reversibility is a hard boundary for our agent: tool actions with side effects cannot be rolled back.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Independent test on realistic web tasks. Best-first search with an LM value function (multimodal GPT-4o, 20 reasoning paths averaged) improves success on VisualWebArena and WebArena. Gains grow with search budget, depth and branching.
numbers: VWA 910 tasks: search improved GPT-4o+SoM by 39.7% relative to a new SOTA of 26.4%. WA 812 tasks: GPT-4o 15.0% to 19.2% (+28.0% relative). Llama-3-70B on WA 7.6% to 10.1% (+32.3%). On 200 VWA tasks, budget c=0 gives 24.5%, c=5 gives 32.0%, c=20 gives 37.0% (+51%). Depth/branch: d=2,b=5 32.0%; d=5,b=5 37.0%.
limits: Search depth limited to 5 actions and budget small for cost. Absolute rates stay low (19.2% on WA), well below specialist agents like AgentOccam (43.1%) that use other tricks. Search is slow, and destructive actions cannot be backtracked in live sites.
agent_relevance: Strongest outside support that search plus an LM value helps with real feedback. Gains scale with budget without a plateau up to c=20, so a modest budget gives most of it. Also shows search does not replace better prompting and observation design.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2025) value function ablation (Table 4)
finding: The quality of the value function sets how much search helps. A strong LM value with many reasoning samples helps most. A weak one helps less. A ground-truth reward helps most of all, showing a large gap to the LM value.
numbers: 200 VWA tasks, GPT-4o agent: no search 24.5%; LLaVA-34B value (SC n=20) 30.0%; GPT-4o value no self-consistency 28.5%; GPT-4o SC n=5 32.5%; GPT-4o SC n=20 37.0%; groundtruth reward 43.5%.
limits: One benchmark subset; value is a prompted LM, not trained. The 6.5-point gap to ground truth shows the value is the bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Directly tells us where to spend: the value step. Averaging several judged samples gave +4.5 points over a single sample (28.5 to 37.0 with n=20). Real checks that return a true reward are better than any LM judge.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: The LM acts as both world model and policy inside MCTS. It lets a 33B model plan Blocksworld far better than chain of thought, which is LATS's closest rival. Its gain on math is modest.
numbers: Blocksworld success (LLaMA-33B): CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00 for 2/4/6 steps; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. GPT-4 CoT beats RAP on 6-step. GSM8K: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP(1) 40.0, RAP(10) 48.6, +aggregation 51.6.
limits: RAP uses LM-simulated states, which costs many more calls than LATS and can drift. On GSM8K RAP(10) is within 2 points of plain self-consistency (46.8 vs 48.6).
agent_relevance: On plain reasoning without external feedback, search over thoughts barely beats voting. Gains are large only where there is a state to track (planning). Supports using search only when the environment returns real signal.

source: Feng et al. (2023) AlphaZero-like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: Prompted LLM value functions are weak. A trained value network is far better. With a trained value, tree search beats greedy decoding, and in deep tasks it beats voting.
numbers: Game24 BFS path@1 with LLaMA-SFT policy: LLaMA prompt value 9.2, GPT-3.5 prompt value (ToT) 21.0, trained LLaMA-V 64.8. GSM8K with GPT-3.5 policy: 72.7 (GPT-3.5 value) vs 74.0 (trained). Path@1: CoT-greedy GSM8K 41.4, BFS-V 52.5; Game24 12.7 vs 64.8. Chess endgame win rate 57.8 vs 96.9 (MCTS-alpha).
limits: Needs training of a value net, which our no-training agent lacks. On small problems (GSM8K, Game24) CoT-SC with a reward model matched or beat tree search at equal tokens (GSM8K CoT-SC ORM 52.3 vs BFS-V 52.5).
agent_relevance: The rival explanation for LATS gains: a good value function, not the tree. With only prompting we have the weak value case (ToT 21.0 on Game24), so search over our own judgments carries the risk shown here.

source: Feng et al. (2023) TS-LLM equal-token comparison
finding: At matched token use, tree search beat self-consistency on some tasks and lost on others. Tree search did better on long-horizon tasks. Self-consistency with a reward model did better on small shallow math.
numbers: Equal-token: PrOntoQA CoT-SC majority 61.1, CoT-SC with ORM 83.2, BFS-V ORM ~ 70.9 on Game24 vs CoT-SC ORM 50.6; chess endgame CoT-SC ORM 73.80 vs BFS-V ORM 93.18. Authors note TS-LLM struggles to improve under large aggregation on GSM8K and Game24.
limits: Authors use trained models and sentence-level nodes. Numbers read from a table whose columns were hard to separate; check the paper table before quoting a single cell.
agent_relevance: Tells us when the tree is worth it: deep, branching tasks with a reliable evaluator. For short tasks, sample and verify is as good and simpler.

source: Wu et al. (2024/2025) Inference Scaling Laws: Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models
finding: At matched compute, MCTS underperformed simple sampling with a reward model on math. A cheaper tree method, REBASE, matched or beat sampling. Smaller models with search were compute-optimal.
numbers: MCTS underperforms sampling-based methods at every compute budget on MATH and GSM8K (Llemma 7B and 34B). MCTS 'often requires dozens of times more generated tokens'. REBASE with 7B reached higher accuracy than sampling weighted voting with about 7 times less compute; Llemma-7B + REBASE beat Llemma-34B with majority voting across budgets.
quote: MCTS underperforms the sampling-based methods at each compute budget
limits: Math word problems with a trained process reward model; not an agent setting with environment feedback. Rollout-based MCTS is the costly part.
agent_relevance: A main failed-boundary result: MCTS with rollouts wastes tokens. If we search, prefer cheap value scoring of nodes over full rollouts, and always compare to best-of-N at equal tokens.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Search against a process reward model helps on medium and hard questions but hurts on easy ones as the budget rises (over-optimisation of the verifier). Lookahead search was the weakest at equal budget.
numbers: Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets, but the gain shrinks and often reverses at large budgets. Budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations. Easy levels 1-2: beam search degrades with budget. Levels 3-4: beam search consistently beats best-of-N. Level 5: no method makes real progress. Lookahead cost counted as N x (k+1). Compute-optimal allocation matched best-of-N with about 4x less compute. Test-time compute beat a 14x larger model on easy and medium questions.
limits: MATH with PaLM 2-S* and a learned PRM; difficulty from the model's own pass rate. Not agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Moderator is difficulty: search should be switched on for mid-hard items, off for easy ones, and gives little on the hardest. Matches our need for a gate before S6. Over-optimising a judge produced short or repetitive junk steps.

source: Huang et al. (2023/2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Reflection gains reported with oracle labels vanish, and turn negative, when the model must judge its own answer. This tests the reflection part of LATS and Reflexion.
numbers: With oracle labels GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. Intrinsic self-correction GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0.
limits: Prompted self-correction on three benchmarks, rounds 1 to 2. Table rows were re-read to map models to numbers. The key pattern (oracle helps, intrinsic hurts) is clear.
agent_relevance: Reflection only helps when a real check says the attempt failed. In LATS the rollout outcome is such a check (test pass, reward). Without it, our agent must not reflect on its own say-so.

source: Olausson et al. (2023/2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: With cost counted, self-repair using test feedback gives small, uneven, and sometimes zero gains over drawing more independent samples. The bottleneck is the quality of the feedback text.
numbers: Repair pass rate relative to equal-budget i.i.d. sampling mostly 0.83 to 1.09, many cells below 1. Human feedback on GPT-4 failing programs: success 52.6% overall vs 33.3% for GPT-4's own feedback (introductory 62.2 vs 42.6; interview 45.7 vs 19.3; competition 14.7 vs 3.7). 16 participants, 40 failing programs, 2 feedbacks each, 25 repair samples per feedback.
limits: Python code, HumanEval and APPS, a one-hour study with 16 people. Ratio table cells from PDF text may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Strong failed-replication of the 'reflection helps' story at equal compute. Search in LATS spends many samples, so its gain over best-of-N must be shown, which this paper says is often absent.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own answers made results worse across Game of 24, Graph Coloring and STRIPS planning, because the verifier made too many false rejections. An external sound verifier gave large gains.
numbers: Game of 24 verifier accuracy 87.0% (3567/4100), false positive rate 10.4% (320/3071), false negative rate 20.7% (213/1029). Blocksworld verifier accuracy 72.4%, FPR 6.5%, FNR 15.48%. Mystery Blocksworld accuracy 71.8%, FPR 18.55%. Performance falls as backprompts increase.
limits: GPT-4 only, a small set of domains; other cells of the table were hard to align in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Core risk for the value function in S6: an LM that scores its own states makes false negatives that prune the right branch. A code check or sound verifier is the safe signal.

source: Antoniades et al. (2024/2025) SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement
finding: MCTS with a hybrid value function (numeric score plus language feedback) and a discriminator debate at the end raised resolve rates on SWE-bench Lite for five different models.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite resolve rate, Moatless-Adapted vs SWE-Search: GPT-4o 25.7 to 31.0 (+17% rel.); GPT-4o-mini 13.0 to 17.0 (+24); Qwen-2.5-72B 18.0 to 24.7 (+27); DeepSeek-V2.5 16.3 to 21.0 (+22); Llama-3.1-70B 13.6 to 17.7 (+23). Mean +23% relative. Original Moatless-v0.0.2 with GPT-4o: 24.3. Max iterations 100, max 3 expansions per node.
limits: Compares to the same agent without search, not to a best-of-N baseline at the same cost. Per-model counts are small subsets of 300 tasks.
agent_relevance: Same direction as LATS in a hard, real-feedback domain (tests). Gains of 4 to 7 points absolute are real but modest. Does not show search beats simply running more attempts.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search: value function versus discriminator
finding: The value function alone picked the correct solution only part of the time. A debate-based discriminator picked it more often. Allowing flexible transitions gave only a tiny gain without search.
numbers: When a correct solution existed, the value function ranked it highest 73% of the time on average over five models; the discriminator raised this to 84%. Moatless-Adapted over Moatless-v0.0.2: only +1.4% (flexible state transitions risk infinite loops).
limits: Average of five models; GPT-4o-mini was an exception where the value function did better than the discriminator.
agent_relevance: Even a good LM value picks the right answer only about 3 times in 4. A final comparison step among candidates gives a measurable extra 11 points. Supports a separate select stage after the search.

source: Putta et al. (2024) Agent Q: Advanced Reasoning and Learning for Autonomous AI Agents
finding: MCTS with a self-critique value, used both at test time and to build DPO data, took web agents far beyond zero-shot. Test-time search by itself gave a large step on a live site.
numbers: WebShop (xLAM base): DPO 28.6%; MCTS on top 48.4%; Agent Q trained 29.5% (+0.9 over DPO); Agent Q + MCTS 50.5%; average human 50.0%. OpenTable live booking (Llama-3-70B): zero-shot 18.6%; RFT 67.2%; GPT-4o zero-shot 62.6%; outcome-only DPO 71.8%; MCTS with outcome Q-values only 75.2%; full Agent Q 81.7%; RFT + MCTS 84.3%; Agent Q + MCTS 95.4%.
limits: Includes training. OpenTable success is judged by a GPT-4-V evaluator, not a hard test. xLAM scored 0.0% on OpenTable. Held-out task counts for WebShop: 1,087 zero-shot tasks.
agent_relevance: Shows an upper bound for search with real feedback, but the 95.4% includes fine-tuning and an LM judge. Search alone on the RFT base gave +17 points (67.2 to 84.3), which is the part we can borrow.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS WebShop analysis
finding: On WebShop, reflections were often generic and gave little. The authors found Reflexion with k=30 trajectories did about as well as ReAct best-of-30, but LATS still improved on both.
numbers: WebShop 50 tasks: ReAct best of k=30 score 59.1 SR 32.0; Reflexion 64.2 / 35.0; LATS 75.9 / 38.0. RL-trained IL+RL baseline 62.4 / 28.7 and 67.5 / 45.0 in the text; fine-tuned expert 82.1 / 59.6; human expert row listed beside.
quote: generated reflections are often generic and do not provide useful feedback
limits: Success rate gain of LATS over Reflexion is only 3 points on 50 tasks (about 1.5 tasks). Large score gain is partial-credit score, not full success. Baselines table was not cleanly separated in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Where the task is hard, reflections are weak and the tree does the work. Success-rate gain is thin, so the headline score gain overstates it.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS Game of 24
finding: On a pure reasoning task without environment feedback, LATS still led its rivals with GPT-3.5, helped by the self-consistency term in its value function.
numbers: Game of 24 success (n=5, k=30): CoT 0.08, Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS (CoT) 0.44. Value mixing: lambda=0.5 gives 0.44; lambda=1 (no self-consistency) gives 0.40.
limits: Authors' own run, GPT-3.5, small gain of 0.04 from the self-consistency term. ToT's own paper reported far higher numbers with GPT-4, so baselines here are weak.
agent_relevance: The self-consistency term adds only a few points. In reasoning-only tasks the gain is mostly from sampling many candidates and picking one.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS programming set-up
finding: On code, LATS generates its own tests and uses their pass rate plus LM score as value. Final choice is scored on the real hidden test suite. The tests give a cheap internal signal.
numbers: HumanEval 164 problems, 8 iterations, n=5 expansions, 4 generated tests (GPT-4) or 6 (GPT-3.5), depth limit 8. GPT-3.5: CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. MBPP GPT-3.5: CoT 54.9, ReAct 67.0, Reflexion 70.0, ToT 65.8, RAP 71.4, LATS 81.1. Authors say LATS scales better than Reflexion with more iterations (Fig. 3).
limits: Generated tests can be wrong; the real test suite is used only at the end. Some baselines use 161 questions of HumanEval. Base GPT-4 80.1.
agent_relevance: Self-made tests are a real-feedback source our agent can use for code. The method still works only if the generated tests are mostly right.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents, limitations
finding: The authors name three limits: search is slow (many more LM calls), destructive actions cannot be undone in a live site, and the value function misjudges some tasks. Success stays low in absolute terms.
numbers: Search tested with depth up to 5 and branching up to 5 and budget up to 20 node expansions per step because of cost. Absolute best result 26.4% on VWA, 19.2% on WA.
limits: Authors' own discussion; no formal cost accounting versus best-of-N.
agent_relevance: Same boundary as LATS: reversibility. Our agent should only search where an action can be simulated or undone, and use a budget cap.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute (revision versus parallel)
finding: Sequential revision helps on easy problems; parallel sampling and tree search help more on hard problems. The best split depends on difficulty and budget.
numbers: Easy questions: sequential revisions beat parallel at low budget. Hard questions: parallel resampling or PRM tree search is better. On the most challenging questions 'very little' benefit from more test-time compute; scaling pretraining is preferable there.
limits: Math only; PaLM 2-S*; revision model fine-tuned for the task.
agent_relevance: For S6, reflection-like revision suits easy items, tree search suits hard ones, and neither saves the hardest. A difficulty gate before choosing is justified by data.

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP ablation and comparison to prompting only
finding: RAP's big Blocksworld gain depends on the model tracking state in text. On the full Blocksworld and with a stronger comparison, the margin shrinks.
numbers: Blocksworld 6-step: RAP(10) 0.26 and RAP(20) 0.42 versus GPT-4 CoT 0.40. Average success for RAP(20) reported as 64%, 33% relative above GPT-4 CoT. CoT pass@10 stayed 0.00 on 6-step, so sampling alone fails where search succeeds.
limits: RAP(10) at 6 steps is below GPT-4 CoT. LLaMA-33B is a weak base model by 2026.
agent_relevance: Rare case where search clearly beats sampling at equal sample count (CoT pass@10 is 0.00 at 6 steps). Needs a world-state description the model can keep correct.

source: Feng et al. (2023) TS-LLM on shallow versus deep search
finding: Alpha-Zero-like search clearly beats greedy decoding where long-horizon planning matters. On shallow trees it only matches baselines.
numbers: RLHF alignment (token-level) reward: CoT greedy 0.318, MCTS-alpha 2.221, MCTS-Rollout 1.925. Chess endgame win rate: CoT greedy 57.8, MCTS-alpha 96.90, MCTS-Rollout 98.76. GSM8K: MCTS-Rollout 47.8 below BFS-V 52.5, with 3.4k vs 485 tokens.
limits: Trained value and ORM; cost grows (MCTS-Rollout 3.4k tokens vs 98 for CoT on GSM8K).
agent_relevance: The benefit of the tree grows with depth of the task. Our shallow decisions probably do not need MCTS.

source: Huang et al. (2023/2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, critique of oracle use
finding: The authors point out that earlier self-correction papers (RCI, Reflexion) used oracle correctness labels to decide when to stop, which makes reported gains unrepresentative of a real run.
numbers: Tests GSM8K, CommonSenseQA and HotpotQA with GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 and GPT-4; max two rounds of self-correction; HotpotQA subset of 100 questions.
quote: improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: The quote is the paper's claim summary in the introduction. Limits: small HotpotQA sample, only two rounds.
agent_relevance: When reading LATS results ask whether the terminal reward is an oracle. In HotPotQA the exact-match reward on a finished answer is one, so the reported gain is an upper bound for a deployed agent.

source: Olausson et al. (2023/2024) Self-Repair, budget accounting
finding: Whether repair wins depends on whether you would have done better by drawing more independent samples at the same compute. Cost-aware plots show repair loses at low budgets and sometimes wins at higher ones with feedback from a stronger model.
numbers: Paper defines a ratio of repair pass rate to i.i.d. pass rate at the same sample budget; cells range about 0.83 to 1.09 in the GPT-3.5/GPT-4 grids shown. Stronger-model feedback gave larger gains, with feedback from a human the largest.
limits: Cell values read from plotted tables; check exact grid before quoting a single value. APPS and HumanEval only.
agent_relevance: Adopt this accounting for any S6 test: report gain per token against best-of-N, not only against one try.

source: Putta et al. (2024) Agent Q value from AI feedback
finding: The MCTS Q value mixes backed-up outcome value and an LM self-critique ranking of candidate actions. Outcome-only Q values already beat plain trajectory DPO, but the added AI feedback gave the extra gain.
numbers: OpenTable: MCTS with outcome-only Q 75.2% vs trajectory DPO 71.8% vs full Agent Q 81.7% (+6.5 over outcome-only). WebShop: process-level supervision gave only +0.9 over DPO because trajectories are short.
limits: Requires training; benefit depends on task length (almost twice as many steps on OpenTable as WebShop).
agent_relevance: Self-critique as a value signal adds a few points on long tasks and almost nothing on short ones. It fits S6 only for long multi-step work.

source: Wu et al. (2024/2025) Inference Scaling Laws, weighted voting versus majority
finding: Theory plus experiments: majority voting accuracy converges to a limit, and a reward-weighted vote has a higher limit. Smaller models are compute-optimal at moderate budgets until their accuracy saturates.
numbers: Llemma-7B beats Llemma-34B until 128 samples are drawn on MATH500; REBASE with 7B beats 34B majority voting at all budgets; tested with weighted majority, best-of-n, and two tree searches.
limits: Math only; PRM used. Conclusions depend on a good reward model.
agent_relevance: Sampling plus a decent scorer is a strong baseline that any agent tree must beat. Our evaluation of S6 should include weighted voting as the control.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) LATS Table 3 rival comparison and n sweep
finding: More children per node improve HotPotQA, with diminishing returns. LATS beat RAP and ToT when each is run with ReAct, so the gain is not just from using the environment.
numbers: HotPotQA EM: LATS n=3 0.58, n=5 0.63, n=10 0.65. ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54. ReAct best of k 0.38.
limits: Authors reimplemented ToT and RAP with ReAct, which can be a handicap for rivals. No independent rerun of these numbers was found in this session.
agent_relevance: A modest branching factor of about 5 gets most of the benefit; going to 10 adds 2 points at double the node cost.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Self-verification: sound verifier baseline
finding: Replacing the LLM critic with an external sound verifier gave substantial gains in every domain, while the LLM critic made performance worse. The effect is about the verifier, not the loop.
numbers: LLM+LLM loop: performance degrades as backprompts increase across Game of 24, Graph Coloring and STRIPS. LLM+Sound Verifier: substantial gains across all domains (figures given per domain in the paper's Figure 2).
limits: Per-domain gains not extracted in this session; only the qualitative direction and the Game of 24 verifier rates are recorded.
agent_relevance: Gives the control for LATS-style value judging: check what happens when the value comes from a sound check. Supports guardrail 'never grade own answer without a check'.

source: Antoniades et al. (2025) SWE-Search, scaling with search iterations
finding: Resolved issues rise as the number of search transitions rises, for all five models. Authors used conservative caps because of cost across 300 instances.
numbers: Max iterations 100 and max 3 expansions per node for the main run; resolved issues grow with transitions (plot). Each model solved some issues no other model solved (Venn overlap).
limits: Caps are far below classic MCTS (thousands of iterations). No curve for best-of-N at the same transitions is given.
agent_relevance: Gains keep coming with budget but the cost is large. Shows value of model diversity: different models solve different issues, so a mix may beat a single model.
